section_title: What becomes of a community when its support and leadership collapse?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 For behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts is about to remove from Jerusalem and Judah both supply and support: the whole supply of food and water, 2 the mighty man and the warrior, the judge and the prophet, the soothsayer and the elder, 3 the commander of fifty and the dignitary, the counselor, the cunning magician, and the clever enchanter. 4 “I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them.” 5 The people will oppress one another, man against man, neighbor against neighbor; the young will rise up against the old, and the base against the honorable.

6 A man will seize his brother within his father’s house: “You have a cloak—you be our leader! Take charge of this heap of rubble.” 7 On that day he will cry aloud: “I am not a healer. I have no food or clothing in my house. Do not make me leader of the people!” 8 For Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because they spoke and acted against the LORD, defying His glorious presence. 9 The expression on their faces testifies against them, and like Sodom they flaunt their sin; they do not conceal it. Woe to them, for they have brought disaster upon themselves.

10 Tell the righteous it will be well with them, for they will enjoy the fruit of their labor. 11 Woe to the wicked; disaster is upon them! For they will be repaid with what their hands have done. 12 Youths oppress My people, and women rule over them. O My people, your guides mislead you; they turn you from your paths.

13 The LORD arises to contend; He stands to judge the people. 14 The LORD brings this charge against the elders and leaders of His people: “You have devoured the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses. 15 Why do you crush My people and grind the faces of the poor?” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts.

context_lines: The warning moves from misplaced trust in people to the removal of the things Judah depends on: food, water, experienced leaders, military strength and counsel. The list also includes people claiming spiritual powers.

The result is disorder and mutual oppression. Leadership becomes so desperate that merely having a cloak seems a reason to be put in charge. The person approached refuses, lacking the resources to repair the ruin.

The passage connects Jerusalem’s condition with words and actions opposed to the Lord. It distinguishes the outcome of the righteous from that of the wicked, then confronts guides who mislead the people.

The Lord stands to bring His charge against elders and leaders. Those who should protect the people have consumed the vineyard and filled their own houses with goods taken from the poor. The accusation names the harm directly: they are crushing God’s people.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/3.htm) understands the would-be healer as someone being asked to repair the ruined state. [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/3.htm) emphasizes the accountability of those entrusted with wealth and power and the particular wrong of making people poor and then oppressing them.

Readings differ about the historical reach of the disaster. The [NABRE notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/isaiah/3) connect the loss of leading people with deportation and the upheaval it causes. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/3.htm) instead directs the passage particularly toward Jerusalem’s later destruction by Rome. The chapter itself names Judah and Jerusalem and makes their rebellion and unjust leadership central to the warning.
